articles.title: Port of Los Angeles sets monthly cargo record
articles.summary: The Port of Los Angeles handled 1,042,652 TEUs in September 2026, the busiest month in the port’s 118-year history, surpassing the previous monthly record set in July 2025 by more than 20,000 units. The record month capped the busiest quarter in port history, with nearly 3 million TEUs handled from July through...
articles.body: The Port of Los Angeles handled 1,042,652 TEUs in September 2026, the busiest month in the port’s 118-year history, surpassing the previous monthly record set in July 2025 by more than 20,000 units. The record month capped the busiest quarter in port history, with nearly 3 million TEUs handled from July through September, while the four-month stretch from June through September produced nearly 4 million TEUs, also the strongest such period on record. Loaded imports reached 545,696 TEUs in September, up 19% year-on-year, while loaded exports totalled 125,751 TEUs, up 10%. Empty containers reached approximately 371,206 TEUs, the highest monthly total in port history. Through the first nine months of 2026, the port has handled nearly 8.1 million TEUs, more than 3% ahead of the same period last year. Executive Director Gene Seroka attributed the record performance to resilient consumer demand, inventory replenishment by importers, and cargo allocation shifting toward Los Angeles as shippers navigate challenges along Suez Canal and Panama Canal routes. He also noted that tariffs are lower than levels seen earlier in the year, giving importers greater cost certainty. Harvard Business School Professor Willy Shih, joining the monthly media briefing, described a broader shift in corporate supply chain strategy from pure cost optimisation toward flexibility in sourcing, manufacturing and cargo routing amid continued global trade uncertainty. Mayor Karen Bass credited the port’s waterfront workforce, the ILWU and Executive Director Seroka for the historic result, describing the port as an extraordinary economic engine supporting good-paying union jobs and maintaining Los Angeles’s status as a global trade and commerce competitor.
takeaways: The Port of Los Angeles handled 1,042,652 TEUs in September 2026, the busiest month in the port’s 118-year history, surpassing the previous monthly record set in July 2025 by more than 20,000 units.
Loaded imports reached 545,696 TEUs in September, up 19% year-on-year, while loaded exports totalled 125,751 TEUs, up 10%.
Empty containers reached approximately 371,206 TEUs, the highest monthly total in port history.

articles.title: Container freight rates weaken as Asia-Europe decline continues
articles.summary: Global container freight rates remained under pressure in the latest weekly readings, with several major benchmarks declining around China’s Golden Week holiday period. Drewry’s World Container Index (WCI) fell 2%, while the China Containerized Freight Index (CCFI) and Ningbo Containerized Freight Index (NCFI) also...
articles.body: Global container freight rates remained under pressure in the latest weekly readings, with several major benchmarks declining around China’s Golden Week holiday period. Drewry’s World Container Index (WCI) fell 2%, while the China Containerized Freight Index (CCFI) and Ningbo Containerized Freight Index (NCFI) also moved lower. The Shanghai Containerized Freight Index (SCFI) was broadly stable, and the Freightos Baltic Index (FBX) recorded almost no change. At trade-lane level, the latest readings showed mixed conditions across the Transpacific, while Asia-Europe continued its downward trend. Chinese freight indexes show mixed performance The SCFI edged up 0.05% to 3,664.11 points, compared with 3,662.30 in the previous reading. The broader CCFI declined 0.6% to 1,912.38 points from 1,923.93. The NCFI also moved lower, falling approximately 1.5% to 2,431.78 points from 2,468.61 in the previous reading. The latest figures show that the Chinese benchmarks remain mixed, although two of the three recorded declines. NYFI highlights diverging Transpacific trends The latest NYSHEX Freight Index (NYFI) , published on 9 October, showed different movements across the two major Asia-US routes. Asia-US West Coast declined 1.98% to 7,407.75, reversing the 1.89% increase recorded in the previous reading. Asia-US East Coast moved in the opposite direction, rising 1.40% to 9,831.24 after remaining almost unchanged in the previous assessment. Asia-North Europe continued to weaken, falling another 3.24% to 3,356.23. The Transatlantic market also showed contrasting movements. Westbound rates edged down 0.52% to 2,709.05, while eastbound rates increased 8.23% to 1,282.09. Charge Current rate New rate Import/Export Fuel Surcharge US$140 per container US$215 per container Scope of the Maersk US inland...
articles.body: Maersk will increase its Import and Export Fuel Surcharge for US inland haulage from 1 November 2026. The Maersk US inland fuel surcharge will rise from US$140 to US$215 per container. Charge Current rate New rate Import/Export Fuel Surcharge US$140 per container US$215 per container Scope of the Maersk US inland fuel surcharge The revised surcharge will apply to shipments carried under a Maersk ocean bill of lading when the carrier arranges trucking to or from the customer’s door within the United States. It will apply to shipments with a Price Calculation Date on or after 1 November 2026. The charge will appear separately on the bill of lading under the IFS or EFS code. Maersk attributed the adjustment to rising US diesel prices. The carrier said the 13-week average diesel price increased by more than US$0.10 per gallon, adding pressure to linehaul, drayage, depot and first-mile transportation costs.
takeaways: Maersk will increase its Import and Export Fuel Surcharge for US inland haulage from 1 November 2026.

articles.title: CMA CGM announces new peak season surcharges on Asia–Africa trades
articles.summary: CMA CGM has announced three Peak Season Surcharges (PSS) on shipments from Asia to Africa, with charges of up to US$750 per TEU taking effect in October 2026. The new surcharges cover shipments from the Far East to Durban, South Africa, from Southeast Asia to northern West Africa, and from China to Mozambique. The...
articles.body: CMA CGM has announced three Peak Season Surcharges (PSS) on shipments from Asia to Africa, with charges of up to US$750 per TEU taking effect in October 2026. The new surcharges cover shipments from the Far East to Durban, South Africa, from Southeast Asia to northern West Africa, and from China to Mozambique. The highest surcharge applies to cargo moving from the Far East to Durban, while the other two trade routes will face additional charges of US$200 per TEU. New surcharge for Durban shipments From 22 October 2026, CMA CGM will apply a PSS of US$750 per TEU on shipments from the Far East to Durban, South Africa. The surcharge applies to all cargo types and will remain in effect until further notice. For shipments originating in China, the charge will be subject to the carrier’s filing with the Shanghai Shipping Exchange and/or may be included in the ocean freight rate. Additional charges for West Africa and Mozambique CMA CGM will also introduce a PSS of US$200 per TEU on shipments from Southeast Asia to northern West Africa, effective 15 October 2026. The surcharge applies to all cargo under short-term contracts. The destinations covered include Liberia, Senegal, Mauritania, Gambia, Guinea, Sierra Leone, Guinea-Bissau, Cape Verde, and São Tomé and Príncipe. Separately, the French shipping company will implement a PSS of US$200 per TEU on shipments from China to Mozambique. This charge will take effect on 22 October 2026 and remain applicable until further notice. It covers all cargo types. As with the Durban surcharge, shipments originating in China will be subject to the relevant Shanghai Shipping Exchange filing requirements and/or inclusion of the PSS in ocean freight. articles.title: HAIAN BETA makes maiden Chennai call
articles.summary: M/V HAIAN BETA made its maiden call at Chennai Port on 3 October 2026, marking the launch of Hai An’s direct CVI service between Vietnam and India. The vessel is the first ship deployed on the new service by Hai An Container Transport Company Limited (HACT), a subsidiary of Hai An Transport and Stevedoring Joint […]
articles.body: M/V HAIAN BETA made its maiden call at Chennai Port on 3 October 2026, marking the launch of Hai An’s direct CVI service between Vietnam and India. The vessel is the first ship deployed on the new service by Hai An Container Transport Company Limited (HACT), a subsidiary of Hai An Transport and Stevedoring Joint Stock Company (HATS). A welcome ceremony for the HAIAN BETA Chennai call took place at Chennai Container Terminal, which is operated by DP World. Representatives attending the event included Sachin S. Kurve, Chairperson of Chennai Port Authority, and Vu Thanh Hai, Chairman of HACT and HATS. Representatives from DP World Chennai and Samsara Shipping, Hai An’s general agent in India, also participated. CVI service links four Asian ports The CVI service operates monthly with the following rotation: Nansha – Hai Phong – Port Klang West – Chennai. The new service establishes an additional direct container shipping connection between Vietnam and India. It also links both markets with major trading hubs in southern China and Malaysia. Hai An said the CVI service is designed to support growing shipping requirements between Vietnam and India. Bilateral trade between the two countries reached US$13.4 billion during the first eight months of 2026, representing a year-on-year increase of 25%. Chennai Port Authority noted that the continued expansion of trade between India and Vietnam is creating further opportunities for container shipping connections between the two markets. The HAIAN BETA Chennai call represents another step in Hai An’s expansion into international container shipping services.
takeaways: M/V HAIAN BETA made its maiden call at Chennai Port on 3 October 2026, marking the launch of Hai An’s direct CVI service between Vietnam and India.
The vessel is the first ship deployed on the new service by Hai An Container Transport Company Limited (HACT), a subsidiary of Hai An Transport and Stevedoring Joint Stock Company (HATS).
A welcome ceremony for the HAIAN BETA Chennai call took place at Chennai Container Terminal, which is operated by DP World.

articles.title: A platform launched to consolidate European port innovation knowledge
articles.summary: The Green Innovation Compass has been launched as a publicly accessible knowledge platform consolidating European expertise on innovative technologies and solutions for the port ecosystem, providing independent and practical insights for all port stakeholders. The platform is one of the key legacy outcomes of the EU...
articles.body: The Green Innovation Compass has been launched as a publicly accessible knowledge platform consolidating European expertise on innovative technologies and solutions for the port ecosystem, providing independent and practical insights for all port stakeholders. The platform is one of the key legacy outcomes of the EU Horizon 2020-funded MAGPIE project, in which the Port of Rotterdam participated alongside ports, companies, knowledge institutions and governments collaborating on innovative solutions for the port of the future. A central lesson from the MAGPIE project was that knowledge about port innovations is often available in fragmented form across different organisations and geographies. The Green Innovation Compass addresses this gap by bringing together research findings, demonstration project results and practical experiences from ports, companies and knowledge institutions across Europe on a single accessible platform. To ensure the long-term continuity of the knowledge platform following the completion of the MAGPIE project, ALICE, the Alliance for Logistics Innovation through Collaboration in Europe, has taken on the role of legacy partner and will maintain and develop the platform going forward.
takeaways: A central lesson from the MAGPIE project was that knowledge about port innovations is often available in fragmented form across different organisations and geographies.

articles.title: Port Houston completes Project 11 Houston ship channel expansion
articles.summary: Port Houston joined federal, state and local officials and industry partners on October 8 to celebrate the completion of Port Houston-led segments of Project 11, the eleventh major expansion of the Houston Ship Channel and one of the most significant infrastructure projects in the waterway’s history. The completed...
articles.body: Port Houston joined federal, state and local officials and industry partners on October 8 to celebrate the completion of Port Houston-led segments of Project 11, the eleventh major expansion of the Houston Ship Channel and one of the most significant infrastructure projects in the waterway’s history. The completed work widened the channel by 170 feet along its Galveston Bay reach, from 530 feet to 700 feet, increasing safety and efficiency along the nation’s busiest waterway. The expanded channel is already delivering operational benefits. In 2025, the US Coast Guard, US Army Corps of Engineers and Houston Pilots recognised the widened 700-foot channel from Bolivar Roads to Morgans Point, effectively removing daylight restrictions for larger vessels transiting Galveston Bay and reducing the need for oversized ships to wait at berth or anchor before sailing. The project was delivered through an innovative funding partnership in which Port Houston and industry partners agreed to contribute financially, cutting years from the delivery timeline. Port Houston completed its portion on time, on budget and faster than any comparable project in the United States. The remainder of project funding came from several federal sources. Project 11 also created lasting environmental benefits through beneficial reuse of all suitable dredged material, producing 10 acres of bird islands, 324 acres of oyster reefs and 800 acres of marsh habitat. articles.title: Readers Speak: Smaller vessels gain favour in container ship orders
articles.summary: As container shipping lines continue to evaluate their fleet expansion strategies, the question of which vessel sizes deserve priority in newbuilding orders remains an important industry consideration. The latest Readers Speak poll by Container News asked readers: “Which vessel size should container lines focus on...
articles.body: As container shipping lines continue to evaluate their fleet expansion strategies, the question of which vessel sizes deserve priority in newbuilding orders remains an important industry consideration. The latest Readers Speak poll by Container News asked readers: “Which vessel size should container lines focus on for new orders?” The results reveal a clear preference for smaller and medium-sized container ships, with Panamax/Post-Panamax and Feeder/Feedermax vessels attracting the strongest support. Meanwhile, Ultra Large Container Vessels (ULCVs) received comparatively limited backing. The findings suggest that readers see considerable value in fleet flexibility and the ability to serve different shipping markets, rather than concentrating new investment primarily on the largest container ships. Panamax and Post-Panamax vessels attract strong support Panamax and Post-Panamax vessels emerged as a leading choice in the latest Readers Speak poll. Their strong showing may reflect the importance readers place on vessels that can operate across a variety of trade routes and service networks. Compared with the largest container ships, these vessel segments offer different deployment possibilities, potentially making them attractive to shipping lines seeking to balance capacity with operational flexibility. The preference also suggests that readers may view medium-sized tonnage as an important component of future fleet development. Rather than prioritising maximum carrying capacity alone, the results point towards an interest in ships that can support a broader range of network requirements. takeaways: As container shipping lines continue to evaluate their fleet expansion strategies, the question of which vessel sizes deserve priority in newbuilding orders remains an important industry consideration.
